message: We're comparing two square building lots. One measures 20 m by 20 m and is listed at $100,000. The other measures 40 m by 40 m and is listed at $200,000. Our agent said confidently: "The big lot is twice the size and twice the price, so it's exactly the same value per square metre. There's no bargain either way." That makes sense to me, since the sides are double. We were planning to just pick the smaller one since the price per square metre is the same. Can we go with this reasoning?
response:
No, the agent's reasoning has a mistake. Doubling the sides of a square doesn't double the area; it multiplies it by four.

| Lot | Area | Price | Price per m² |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 m × 20 m | 400 m² | $100,000 | **$250** |
| 40 m × 40 m | 1,600 m² | $200,000 | **$125** |

The large lot is four times the size for twice the price, so it costs **half as much per square metre**. If price per square metre is your measure, the large lot is clearly the better deal.

That doesn't mean you have to buy it. The smaller lot may still be the right choice if:
- **$100,000 is your budget.** A lower price per m² only helps if you can afford the total.
- **You don't need the extra land.** Extra space you won't use isn't really value. It can also add property tax and upkeep.
- **The lots aren't equivalent.** Location, slope, access, services, setback rules and how much area you can actually build on often matter more than raw size.

So choose the smaller lot if it suits your needs, but not because it's equal value. On price per square metre, the larger lot is twice as good a deal.
